Leicestershire batsman Harry Dearden told BBC Radio Leicester:
"I was very proud to get a career-best, I would have loved to have got to three figures but still very proud, it's been a really good day for us.
"It was doing a bit early on, nipping around and swinging, you've just got to take as many balls as you can to get in and it was a good battle up top.
"I just tried to knuckle down and be as disciplined as I could. It's good batting with Horts (Paul Horton), he's an experienced head and calms you down, and it's really good batting with Mark (Pettini), he keeps you level."
Glamorgan spinner Andrew Salter told BBC Wales Sport:
"I am happy to take those two wickets, though it won't come as a surprise that they didn't turn that much- one through the gate and one a bit fuller that hit a bit of rough.
"It was more about trying to control the run-rate and I felt that if I built enough pressure there'd be some reward at the end of it, so hopefully I won't be needed too much more in the first innings.
"For the majority of the day we bowled really well as a group, Lukas (Carey) bowled amazingly up top, the run-rate was 2.6 for most of the day and it wasn't until the end that they got away from us."

Nineteen-year-old Dearden proved instrumental for Leicestershire, commencing his innings with an 85-run opening partnership alongside Paul Horton (41). Following a rapid loss of three wickets, two claimed by the young Lukas Carey, Dearden reasserted control, establishing a 90-run stand with Mark Pettini, who remained unbeaten on 63. Under floodlights, Pettini's contribution also secured the Foxes' second batting point. Dearden's substantial knock of 145, a cornerstone for his team's first innings total and a formidable challenge for Glamorgan, was not without its moments of peril; he survived an early dropped catch on just one run and narrowly avoided being run out on multiple occasions. This resilient century, showcasing his burgeoning talent, featured 18 fours and two sixes, and spanned over five hours at the crease. His time at the wicket unfolded in two distinct phases: an initial cautious approach against the new ball, followed by an aggressive acceleration with Pettini that put Glamorgan under significant pressure. These early close calls seemingly bolstered his determination to convert his start into a substantial score. His exceptional solo effort concluded when spinner Andrew Salter dislodged him with a sharply turning delivery, representing a momentary lapse in his otherwise steadfast concentration.

With Dearden's departure, Leicestershire required ongoing solidity. Mark Pettini, who had provided vital support, seamlessly stepped into the role of chief aggressor. He then forged a productive partnership with Ned Eckersley, and together they systematically advanced the foundation laid by Dearden. Despite previous breakthroughs, Glamorgan's bowling attack struggled to break through Pettini's experienced defense. Lukas Carey, though at times expensive, persistently troubled batsmen with his express pace and bounce, while Andrew Salter's precise left-arm spin aimed to restrict scoring. Yet, as the floodlit conditions increasingly favoured batting, the Welsh team's bowlers found it difficult to sustain consistent pressure.

As stumps approached, Pettini celebrated a commendable century, propelling Leicestershire beyond the 400-run threshold. At 415 for 7, they declared their innings, allowing their bowlers a brief opportunity to challenge Glamorgan's openers before the end of the day's play. This was a clear strategic maneuver, designed to put immediate pressure on Glamorgan. Facing a demanding 10-over spell under the floodlights, Glamorgan's opening pair, Sam Northeast and Nick Selman, initially stood firm. However, Leicestershire's new-ball attack, spearheaded by Chris Wright, exerted relentless pressure. Glamorgan ended the day at 28 for 1, with Selman falling cheaply, caught at slip from an excellent delivery by Gavin Griffiths. Northeast (15*) and Marnus Labuschagne (8*) are set to continue tomorrow, with Glamorgan trailing by a significant 387 runs. The game remains delicately balanced; Leicestershire holds a distinct advantage thanks to Dearden's exceptional knock and Pettini's solid finish, yet Glamorgan must lean on their strong batting order to counter on what appears to be an accommodating pitch. The British Film Institute (BFI) has recently introduced a vast online archive, making available previously unseen footage that offers a comprehensive view of Ulster's history. This significant cultural initiative, 'From Britain On Film,' now grants the public free access to hundreds of unique films. The collection vividly illustrates diverse aspects of Ulster life, ranging from Winston Churchill's notable 1912 visit to Belfast and a 1963 re-enactment of a Viking invasion in a County Down fishing village, to narratives of tourism, industrial heritage, and sports. While formal events such as royal tours and Lord Mayor's processions historically offered glimpses into the region's public ceremonies, this newly available material provides a much deeper understanding. It serves as an essential lens into Ulster's societal structure. Beyond official parades and prominent political figures, viewers can explore the bustling activity of Belfast's docks, the skilled craftsmanship of linen manufacturers, and the lively atmosphere of street markets. The daily lives of ordinary citizens are also brought to light, featuring children at play, families enjoying beach holidays, and communities gathering for local festivities.

Curated by the BFI, this extraordinary compilation spans over a century, documenting moments of national significance, local customs, industrial development, and social transformations. The footage itself is remarkably varied, including early silent films of horse-drawn trams in urban areas, post-war documentaries showcasing agricultural progress in County Armagh, and the expanding tourism along the Antrim Coast. Together, these films form a dynamic historical record of the province, illuminating the impact of both major events and daily routines, thus portraying a society in transition, adapting to industrialization and evolving social norms.

Through these films, audiences can trace the evolution of industries, from Belfast's shipbuilding prowess to the intricate art of lacemaking. The growth of infrastructure, towns, and rural communities is thoroughly chronicled. Sporting events, encompassing everything from local Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) matches to international rugby encounters, receive prominent attention, celebrating Ulster's rich sporting legacy. More than mere historical documentation, these films offer evocative insights into the past, revealing the aspirations, hardships, and celebrations of previous generations.

By making hundreds of these unique films available online, the British Film Institute (BFI) has preserved a vital component of the UK's cinematic heritage and established an invaluable resource for historians, researchers, and anyone interested in Ulster's way of life. This project truly animates a rich collection of experiences, offering unique perspectives on a region often primarily recognized for its political narrative, yet here depicted through its diverse everyday life and environments. Encompassing everything from grave subjects to lighthearted moments, from public spectacles to quiet daily routines, this archive encourages us to explore the many facets of Ulster’s past, culminating in a comprehensive and deeply human account. The inclusion of early footage, such as Winston Churchill's 1912 visit to Belfast, strongly underscores film's long-standing role in documenting significant regional historical moments, thereby contributing to this unparalleled visual record.

From Winston Churchill's infamous visit to Belfast in 1912 to a 1963 Viking invasion re-enactment in a County Down fishing town, as well as tales of tourism, industrial heritage and sport, a dazzling mosaic of Ulster life is pieced together in unseen archive footage.
Hundreds of unique films have been released to the public to view online for free after the British Film Institute (BFI) unlocked its archive as part of a major history project, From Britain On Film.
Royal visits and Lord Mayor's shows are documented in the collection, as is the tale of Churchill's appearance in Belfast when he addressed an audience of nationalists in Celtic Park and gave his support to Home Rule.
There are also dozens of travelogues that were used to sell Northern Ireland to tourists in Great Britain and the United States, helping to boost tourism in the years before the Troubles.
And in sport, the 1930 Ulster Tourist Trophy race held at the Ards circuit in County Down is captured on camera. The event attracted thousands of spectators and commanded the attention of the motorsport world.
The real gems, however, are found in the footage of ordinary people doing extraordinary things.
Films of people at work in the spinning mills and constructing the M1 at Stockman's Lane in Belfast shows Northern Ireland's industry at its booming best.
Another film captures the first time Northern Ireland hosted the World Ploughing Championships, and fittingly it is a local man who takes the title.
The colour footage from the 1959 competition in Armoy, County Antrim, shows Lawrence McMillan's crowning moment as he gets his hands on the Golden Plough.
But perhaps most revealing of all is a 1938 recording of the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast.
It gives a rare glimpse into the casualty department and operating theatres as they were then, 10 years before the foundation of the National Health Service.
While medicine has advanced considerably in the eight decades since then, some aspects of healthcare in Northern Ireland appear to remain unchanged - the film ends with an appeal from the chairman of the hospital's management board to reduce waiting lists.
Francis Jones, of Northern Ireland Screen, which gathered much of the footage, said the aim of the project was to preserve delicate film that could otherwise be lost.
"There is a pure nostalgia value to film. It's different to reading a textbook or history book," he added.
"To actually see the film has that kind of visceral appeal and really strikes a chord with people."
The full From Britain On Film archive can be viewed at the BFI Player.

Recent findings from the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing indicate an increasing number of people under 25 are choosing anti-wrinkle injections. Medical professionals warn that this trend risks creating "frozen faces," potentially impairing young individuals' natural ability to convey emotions. BAAPS, a leading UK medical organization, has declared cosmetic injections for teenagers to be "morally wrong." Treatments like Botox achieve their effect by temporarily immobilizing muscles in the upper facial area, thereby diminishing wrinkles that commonly appear with expressions such as frowning.

Helen Collier, the nurse practitioner behind the study, attributes this worrying development primarily to reality TV and social media. She notes that young clients often emulate the seemingly perfect, frequently filtered images widespread across digital platforms and mainstream media, leading to unattainable beauty ideals. Collier, whose research is featured in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing, voiced significant apprehension regarding the psychological impact of disrupting a developing brain's emotional expression and comprehension. She explained that the muscles affected by Botox are vital for expressing a full range of human emotions, beyond just frowning, encompassing everything from surprise to sadness. Prolonged paralysis of these muscles from a young age might hinder an individual's authentic emotional experience and communication, potentially compromising their social growth and emotional intelligence.

Furthermore, the research highlights a change in motivations: while older patients generally use Botox to reduce existing wrinkles, younger people are increasingly opting for "preventative Botox" to prevent wrinkles from forming at all. This new justification raises substantial ethical concerns for medical practitioners. Ms. Collier contends that securing truly informed consent from teenagers is challenging, due to their still-developing brains and possible difficulty in fully understanding the lasting consequences of such treatments. She stressed that cosmetic choices, particularly those like Botox, demand a mature evaluation of potential risks and rewards, a skill often lacking in those under 25.

BAAPS has reiterated these worries, reaffirming its strong stance against cosmetic injections for individuals under 18, describing the practice as "morally indefensible." For the 18-to-25 age group, BAAPS recommends utmost prudence and a comprehensive psychological assessment prior to any procedure. The association advocates for mental health and a healthy body image, advising against treatments that could have lasting negative effects on a young person's self-image and emotional development.

Collier's study, also published in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing, implores clinicians to place the mental well-being and developmental requirements of younger patients first. She calls for more stringent rules concerning the marketing and administration of cosmetic injectables to minors and young adults, proposing that compulsory waiting periods and psychological evaluations be made routine. She suggests that medical professionals bear a duty to safeguard susceptible individuals from potential damage, which includes declining to yield to commercial incentives to provide treatments that may not serve the patient's best interests. The research underscores an pressing societal imperative to transcend the continuous quest for an artificially perfect appearance, instead promoting genuine beauty and strong self-esteem among young people, domestically and worldwide. This necessitates informing both healthcare providers and the public about the full extent and potential drawbacks of treatments like Botox, to guarantee thoughtful decisions and to ensure the emotional and psychological safety of youth is paramount. The broader, long-term consequences of Botox application in this age group on shared emotional comprehension and non-verbal communication are still unquantified, heightening the concerns of experts like Helen Collier.

Writing in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing, clinicians say there is a growing trend for under-25s to seek the wrinkle-smoothing injections.
But the research suggests "frozen faces" could stop young people from learning how to express emotions fully.
A leading body of UK plastic surgeons says injecting teenagers for cosmetic reasons is "morally wrong".
Botox and other versions of the toxin work by temporarily paralysing muscles in the upper face to reduce wrinkling when people frown.
Nurse practitioner Helen Collier, who carried out the research, says reality TV shows and celebrity culture are driving young people to idealise the  "inexpressive frozen face."
But she points to a well-known psychological theory, the facial feedback hypothesis, that suggests adolescents learn how best to relate to people by mimicking their facial expressions.
She says: "As a human being our ability to demonstrate a wide range of emotions is very dependent on facial expressions.
"Emotions such as empathy and sympathy help us to survive and grow into confident and communicative adults."
But she warns that a "growing generation of blank-faced" young people could be harming their ability to correctly convey their feelings.
"If you wipe those expressions out, this might stunt their emotional and social development," she says.
The research calls for practitioners to use assessment tools to decide whether there are clear clinical reasons for Botox treatment.
Several assessment scales exist that take into account how thick the skin is, how sun-damaged it appears, and the depth of any wrinkles, but experts warn that some Botox clinics are putting financial gain first.
Ms Collier calls on therapists to spend time helping young people boost their confidence rather than reaching for injections.
She adds: "Though most of the effects of the toxin are temporary, research suggests the muscles don't fully recover from injections.
"We really need to understand the consequences of starting treatments too soon."
Dr Michael Lewis, a researcher in psychology at Cardiff University, says: "The expressions we make on our face affect the emotions we feel.
"We smile because we are happy, but smiling also makes us happy.
"Treatment with drugs like Botox prevents the patient from being able to make a particular expression and can therefore have an effect on our learning to feel emotions naturally."
Rajiv Grover, president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, says: "Injecting teenagers with Botox for cosmetic purposes is morally wrong and something that no ethical practitioner would do.
"This can only exacerbate body image issues at a vulnerable time."
Ms Collier's research will be presented at the Clinical Cosmetic and Reconstructive Expo in October.

These narcotics were transported from Colombia to various European nations, predominantly using sailing vessels. Officials confirmed the suspects played key roles in a vast transatlantic drug enterprise orchestrated by the 'Ndrangheta, a formidable organized crime syndicate originating from Calabria, southern Italy. These transatlantic journeys often involved strategic stopovers at island nations for resupply before the narcotics reached their European endpoints, primarily ports in Spain and Portugal, for subsequent distribution throughout the continent. This specific operation was the successful outcome of extensive, multi-year intelligence collection and a cooperative endeavor involving numerous law enforcement bodies.

Utilizing the DEA's valuable insights, law enforcement agencies in Colombia and Italy, with support from Europol and other European police forces, executed synchronized raids. These arrests targeted key logistical facilitators across Europe and several primary suppliers in South America. The captured Farc commander in Colombia was instrumental, reportedly overseeing the cocaine's quality and quantity, and arranging its delivery to coastal collection points. Klitschko added, "This extends beyond boxing; it’s about basic human decency and mutual respect." By prioritising green infrastructure and active transportation, they are not merely enhancing the daily lives of those on campus but also positively influencing the health and prosperity of the broader region. This project will reinforce their standing as a leading urban university, deeply embedded in Sheffield & South Yorkshire, committed to building a better future for its residents and natural environment.

RMT General Secretary Mick Cash strongly criticized the announcement, describing it as a "significant blow" to both employees and the general public. He guaranteed that all current guards and their managers would be reassigned to new platform-based roles interacting with passengers, retaining their salaries and avoiding any forced job losses. Tilley argued that this change would enhance passenger experience and align with prevailing UK railway industry standards. He urged the RMT to engage cooperatively and forgo disruptive industrial action, which would negatively impact daily commuters and the local economy.

Speaking to BBC Newcastle, Durham's head coach, Jon Lewis, expressed profound disappointment, acknowledging his squad was "a long way short" of expectations. He emphasized that even in a reduced-overs fixture, scoring just 90 runs from 22 overs was "not good enough." Lewis pointed out that top-order batsmen are typically relied upon to establish a solid start when chasing a low total, but the team "never got going." He characterized the entire game as an "exceptionally poor performance," especially as the playing conditions improved. Lewis admitted that despite anticipating Worcestershire's aggressive approach, his team "simply crumbled under the pressure." He found the result "frustrating," particularly given their stronger showings in other Riverside matches, viewing it as a "significant regression."

Captain Scott Borthwick echoed these sentiments, stating this was "certainly not what they aimed for." He highlighted thorough preparation that was undermined by a critical "lapse in execution." The early fall of wickets placed them at an insurmountable disadvantage. He credited Worcestershire for their "exceptionally well" bowling, which applied "constant pressure." Borthwick underscored the urgent necessity to "learn from this quickly" and "bounce back strongly" in their next fixture. He reaffirmed the squad's inherent talent and potential for improved performances, vowing to "address the issues" and "come back stronger."

Key fast bowler Chris Rushworth also conveyed his dismay. He attributed their struggles partly to "dropping catches and misfields at crucial moments," which "gave away too many easy runs" while they simultaneously "failed to make enough themselves." "The guys have accepted that something has to change, whether it's the way we approach it, or the way guys practice."
A four-and-a-half-hour rain delay saw the game reduced to 22 overs a side, but Durham's score was their lowest against Worcestershire since becoming a first-class county in 1992.
Only Mark Stoneman and Paul Collingwood made it to double figures with 29 and 17 respectively.

Papua New Guinea's highest court recently delivered a pivotal judgment, declaring the Manus Island detention center unconstitutional. This significant legal decision effectively invalidated a long-standing inter-governmental agreement, immediately prompting widespread discussions and diplomatic efforts. For many years, Manus Island has been a core component of Australia's controversial offshore processing scheme, where asylum claims were assessed beyond Australian borders. In response to this crucial verdict, Papua New Guinea has officially pledged to close the facility, although the precise timeline and operational specifics for this undertaking are still being reviewed.

Established in 2001, Manus Island has, like other remote Australian offshore centers, consistently held a central and frequently contested position within Australia's broader asylum framework. Charles Lepani, PNG's high commissioner to Australia, clarified that the upcoming closure of the Manus Island facility would be a phased, rather than immediate, process. He emphasized the critical need for robust cooperation and joint action with Australia to ensure the humane and respectful transfer of all asylum seekers currently housed at the site. This far-reaching legal decision has placed both nations in a delicate and challenging predicament, necessitating astute diplomatic engagement and strategic negotiations to resolve the intricate human rights and political dilemmas at hand. Lepani reaffirmed PNG's profound regard for the court's judgment, while also prioritizing the welfare, safety, and human dignity of those held there throughout the process. Although a definite date for its complete shutdown has not been established, he confirmed it would not happen abruptly and requires thorough preparation.

Continuous and productive discussions are therefore vital for developing and implementing a sustainable, long-term resolution for the hundreds of vulnerable men caught in prolonged limbo. The controversial "Pacific Solution" arrangement, which involved Australia regularly sending asylum seekers to Manus, has long faced widespread international disapproval and sharp criticism from human rights organizations globally. The Supreme Court's explicit finding that indefinite detention on Manus infringed upon asylum seekers' constitutional right to personal freedom unequivocally binds both governments to confront the grave moral, ethical, and legal ramifications of this scrutinized policy. This momentous judicial verdict starkly illustrates the inherent tension that often exists between national security measures, such as border protection, and the imperative to uphold basic human rights.

Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's administration quickly recognized the pivotal judgment and publicly committed to collaborating closely with Papua New Guinea to manage the intricate transition. Nevertheless, Australia maintains its unwavering policy: no asylum seekers processed on Manus Island will ever be permitted to settle in Australia. This resolute position significantly exacerbates an already difficult situation, as long-term resettlement possibilities in other nations are limited, creating a deep humanitarian predicament. Charles Lepani has urged broader international cooperation and substantial backing from global allies to find genuinely sustainable and compassionate resolutions, suggesting that the international community bears a collective responsibility in resolving what he has labeled an urgent humanitarian crisis.

As a result, the destiny of the Manus facility, and indeed Australia's entire offshore processing scheme, continues to be highly ambiguous, pending further political and legal shifts. Both the Australian and PNG governments are facing increasing pressure to swiftly provide clarity and durable, humane solutions for all individuals deeply impacted by these circumstances. This pivotal ruling emphasizes the enduring importance of an independent judiciary in courageously safeguarding fundamental human rights, even when these decisions challenge complex agreements between nations. Given the protracted and complex nature of this persistent challenge, coupled with the absence of immediate, simple solutions, the facility's actual closure is anticipated to be a meticulously planned, multi-stage endeavor. This will necessarily require considerable diplomatic efforts, intricate logistical planning, and significant inter-governmental teamwork. Papua New Guinea maintains its steadfast dedication to upholding its legal and constitutional obligations stemming from the court's decision, while also striving to preserve and strengthen its enduring, strong bilateral ties with Australia. The international community watches attentively, awaiting concrete and decisive measures to effectively address this persistent and deeply concerning humanitarian situation. Ultimately, the immediate safety, security, and eventual dignified resettlement of all detainees serve as the clear primary objective and guiding principle for every party involved in this intricate affair.

Leigh Halfpenny's existing contract with French club Toulon is scheduled to conclude in mid-2016. There is growing speculation that his former team, the Cardiff Blues, is actively pursuing his return to Welsh rugby. The 26-year-old full-back initially moved from the Blues to France in 2014. Coach Pivac confirmed the club's interest, stating they would be keen to speak with Halfpenny if he genuinely wished to return, treating him no differently from any other prospective player. Pivac further stressed the financial realities, mentioning that their budget was not unlimited and his previous statements on the matter still stood. These candid remarks from Pivac serve to highlight the ongoing economic limitations and financial realities confronting the Welsh regional rugby landscape. While the Cardiff Blues are undoubtedly eager to acquire a player of Halfpenny's calibre, any prospective agreement would have to meticulously fit within the region's stringent budgetary constraints. Given Halfpenny's position as one of European rugby's highest earners at Toulon, a substantial and challenging reduction in his income would almost certainly be required to facilitate any potential return to Arms Park. His estimated annual salary with the French club, between £600,000 and £700,000, is a figure well beyond the realistic financial capacity of any Welsh region.

Since his transfer to Toulon, the Welsh international and British & Irish Lions full-back has been exceptionally successful, rapidly establishing himself as a crucial member of their formidable squad. His precise goal-kicking, formidable defensive prowess, and consistently courageous play on the field have collectively made him an indispensable part of the Top 14 and European champion Toulon squad. However, a severe knee injury, sustained during a Rugby World Cup warm-up in September 2015, has sidelined him for the majority of the current season, causing considerable uncertainty regarding his short-term playing prospects and his full rehabilitation timeline. Despite this setback, his market value remains extremely high, with Toulon reportedly keen to retain his services and having offered a lucrative new contract. Halfpenny's ultimate decision will undoubtedly involve a careful balancing act, weighing the considerable allure of the intense, financially rewarding environment of French club rugby against a profound desire to return to Wales, potentially with a strategic focus on the 2019 Rugby World Cup and a personal wish to be nearer to his family.

For the Cardiff Blues, Halfpenny's potential return would signify a major triumph, bringing benefits both on the pitch and commercially. His presence would offer not only extensive experience at rugby's highest echelons but also elite kicking ability and an undeniable offensive threat operating from the crucial full-back position. More importantly, his comeback would significantly enhance the region's public image and overall marketability, with the potential to attract larger crowds to matches and open up entirely new avenues for sponsorship opportunities. Pivac has frequently emphasized the strategic necessity for the Blues to cultivate a robust team built on a strong Welsh foundation, carefully enhanced by key international players for added depth and quality. Halfpenny, having progressed through the Blues' academy before gaining senior international recognition, would be an ideal fit for this particular strategy.

The primary and arguably most significant hurdle for the Blues' leadership will be crafting a truly persuasive argument for Halfpenny, one that extends well beyond mere monetary aspects and appeals to other crucial motivations. They would need to emphasize the compelling prospect of playing consistent rugby in Wales, taking on a pivotal role in the ongoing redevelopment efforts at Arms Park, and crucially, the enhanced opportunity to be more closely integrated into the Welsh national squad setup – an aspect that often proves more challenging for players based overseas in foreign leagues. While other Welsh regions, such as the Ospreys, might also express interest if Halfpenny ultimately decides to return to Wales, the Cardiff Blues would, in all likelihood, possess a considerable and perhaps decisive edge, given his deep-seated past connections and undeniable fondness for the very team where his illustrious professional journey first commenced. The upcoming months are therefore set to be absolutely vital as Halfpenny carefully considers his array of choices, with the wider rugby community keenly observing precisely where one of the sport's most coveted and influential talents will opt to continue his distinguished career after the 2016 season. Indeed, the anticipated discussions between the player and the Blues, as confirmed by Coach Pivac, will prove instrumental in ultimately deciding if a sentimental and practical return home is truly feasible for the Gwent-born athlete.

Aaron Ramsey, an Arsenal FC midfielder aged 24 at the time, uploaded an image from his 2014 wedding. The accompanying Welsh caption, "un flwyddyn heddiw," translates directly to "one year today." Though some comments were positive, a significant number of social media users reacted with confusion or derision, with one individual even asking if the FA Cup victor was "intoxicated."

The core of this widespread misunderstanding lay in a literal interpretation of the Welsh idiom. "Un flwyddyn heddiw" functions as a standard, idiomatic Welsh phrase for commemorating an anniversary, meaning precisely "one year today" since the event occurred. Nevertheless, numerous English-speaking users on social media overlooked these inherent linguistic and cultural subtleties, taking the phrase at face value. Ramsey, proudly Welsh, had posted the photograph from his 2014 nuptials on what was undeniably their first anniversary in 2015. Consequently, some users wrongly inferred the caption referred to the photograph's age, an assumption illogical for an image depicting a 2014 wedding. Others struggled to reconcile a 2014 occasion with a "one year today" caption, prompting them to conclude he was mistaken about when he got married.

Ramsey's decision to communicate in his mother tongue, a common practice for him, was extensively misconstrued. For instance, Twitter user @rightjudgeiam sarcastically remarked, "Does Aaron Ramsey not know how long a year is? 2014 wedding, posts 'one year today'. Welsh or not, that's just bad maths." Such responses revealed a fundamental lack of awareness regarding the typical application of anniversary salutations in Welsh culture. The ensuing mockery frequently stemmed from the belief that he was suggesting his 2014 marriage had taken place only "one year today" in relation to his 2015 upload. This incident vividly illustrated the inherent challenges of digital platforms, where vital context, linguistic distinctions, and cultural nuances are readily missed, turning a straightforward, culturally embedded message into material for widespread online jest and derision.

A comprehensive six-year investigation, published in BMC Medicine, involving over 200,000 Australians aged 45 and above, encompassing both tobacco users and non-smokers, unveiled a clear connection between cigarette consumption and an elevated likelihood of premature demise. The research indicated that merely smoking ten cigarettes daily was associated with a twofold increase in this fatal risk, while individuals consuming twenty cigarettes a day faced a four to five times higher probability of dying earlier. Although some smokers may experience extended lifespans, their habit markedly diminishes this prospect. This study highlighted the profound impact of even moderate tobacco use on mortality rates, affirming decades of prior evidence regarding the dangers of smoking and linking it to a broad spectrum of health problems, including various cancers, cardiovascular conditions, and respiratory ailments.

While lung cancer is arguably the most commonly recognized consequence, tobacco use also considerably amplifies the chances of developing cancers of the throat, mouth, esophagus, bladder, kidney, pancreas, stomach, and cervix, in addition to acute myeloid leukemia. Beyond malignant diseases, smokers contend with substantially heightened risks of heart attacks, strokes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), emphysema, and bronchitis. Furthermore, smoking plays a role in the onset of type 2 diabetes, age-related macular degeneration (a condition that can lead to vision loss), and osteoporosis, which causes bones to weaken.

Professor Emily Banks, a lead investigator in the BMC Medicine project, underscored that even minimal daily smoking carries substantial mortality consequences. Her findings, which align with insights from other major health organizations, point to an undeniable dose-response relationship between cigarette intake and adverse health outcomes. Institutions such as Cancer Research UK and the American Cancer Society have long spearheaded public health initiatives aimed at curbing smoking prevalence, emphasizing that many tobacco-related illnesses are preventable. Despite significant progress in reducing smoking rates in the United Kingdom, tobacco remains a primary contributor to early death and disease within the country.

Medical professionals universally agree that discontinuing smoking at any juncture markedly improves health prospects and extends one's lifespan, thereby mitigating the elevated dangers associated with continued tobacco use. Even for those who have smoked for many years, stopping the habit initiates a process of physical recovery and risk reduction that can add years to life and enhance overall well-being. The evidence is conclusive: every cigarette harms the body, making the decision to quit one of the most beneficial actions an individual can undertake for their personal health.

The study tracked more than 200,000 Australian smokers and non-smokers above the age of 45 over six years.
Mortality risk went up with cigarette use, BMC Medicine reports.
Smoking 10 cigarettes a day doubled the risk, while 20-a-day smokers were four to five times more likely to die.
Although someone who smokes could lead a long life, their habit makes this less likely.
Smoking increases the risk of a multitude of health problems, including heart disease and cancer.
Cancer Research UK currently advises that half of all long-term smokers eventually die from cancer or other smoking-related illnesses.
But recent evidence suggests the figure may be higher.
Newer studies in UK women, British doctors and American Cancer Society volunteers have put the figure at up to 67%, says Prof Emily Banks, lead author of the Australian study.
"We knew smoking was bad, but we now have direct independent evidence that confirms the disturbing findings that have been emerging internationally.
"Even with the very low rates of smoking that we have in Australia, we found that smokers have around threefold the risk of premature death of those who have never smoked. We also found smokers will die an estimated 10 years earlier than non-smokers," she said.
George Butterworth, tobacco policy manager at Cancer Research UK, said: "It's a real concern that the devastation caused by smoking may be even greater than we previously thought.
"Earlier research has shown, as a conservative estimate, one in two long-term smokers die from smoking-related diseases in the UK, but these new Australian figures show a higher risk.
"Smoking habits differ between Australia and the UK [in terms of] how much people smoke and the age they start, so we can't conclude that the two-in-three figure necessarily applies to the UK."
In Australia, about 13% of adults smoke. In the UK, the figure is about 20%.
Stopping smoking can bring a person's health risks back down.
Ten years after quitting, risk of lung cancer falls to half that of a smoker and risk of heart attack falls to the same as someone who has never smoked, according to NHS Smokefree.

Rehtaeh Parsons, 17, of Nova Scotia, killed herself in April after being taunted over a photo of her alleged rape by four boys, her mother has said.

One of the men was charged with two counts of distribution of child pornography, the other with one count each of making child pornography and distribution of child pornography.
The RCMP said the names of the accused would not be released because they were youths at the time of the alleged offence, and warned Halifax residents who believe they know the identities of the accused not to release them on penalty of prosecution, nor to take vigilante action.

"She was never left alone," Ms Parsons told CBC News in April after Rehtaeh's suicide.
"Her friends turned against her, people harassed her, boys she didn't know started texting her and Facebooking asking her to have sex with them since she had had sex with their friends. It just never stopped."

Seventeen-year-old Nova Scotian Rehtaeh Parsons tragically died by suicide in April, a devastating event attributed to severe harassment she endured. This harassment stemmed from a photograph that her mother alleged depicted her sexual assault by four boys. Following a reopened inquiry, two 18-year-old males were taken into custody on Thursday in connection with the image. The identities of these individuals are being withheld, as they are slated to appear in a juvenile court. Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) Superintendent Roland Wells, speaking at a press conference in Halifax that day, voiced his hope that these arrests would "contribute to the healing process within the community."

Superintendent Wells, who oversees support services for the Nova Scotia RCMP, stressed that the investigation remains active and ongoing, urging anyone with pertinent information to come forward. He extended his gratitude to the public for their patience and cooperation throughout the comprehensive review. These arrests signify a major breakthrough in a case that has garnered both national and international attention, inciting widespread outrage and prompting a critical re-evaluation of Canada's legal frameworks concerning cyberbullying and the sharing of non-consensual intimate images.

The decision to make arrests resulted from a thorough re-examination of the case by the RCMP. This new review was launched after an initial investigation by the Halifax Regional Police concluded in February without any charges being laid. That prior outcome had been met with strong condemnation from Rehtaeh's family, victim advocacy groups, and the public, which led to a direct plea for intervention from the Nova Scotia government. Premier Darrell Dexter had personally apologized to Rehtaeh’s mother, Leah Parsons, for the initial handling of the case and formally requested that the RCMP take over the inquiry.

Leah Parsons has tirelessly championed justice for her daughter. She has used social media platforms and media interviews to share Rehtaeh’s story, underscoring the destructive impacts of online harassment. Ms. Parsons has consistently advocated for more robust legal measures and a more empathetic approach from law enforcement and the justice system towards survivors of sexual assault. Rehtaeh's tragic experience quickly became emblematic of the urgent need for action against online violence, sparking a national dialogue on consent, privacy, and the responsibilities of both internet users and service providers.

The two arrested individuals are facing charges related to the distribution of an intimate image, which allegedly showed Rehtaeh's sexual assault. Due to their age at the time of the alleged offense and specific provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act, their names cannot be publicly disclosed. Their forthcoming prosecution in a juvenile court highlights the inherent challenges of applying existing laws to evolving forms of digital crime.

The Nova Scotia community, particularly in Halifax, has been profoundly affected by Rehtaeh’s death. Numerous vigils, protests, and online campaigns have called for justice and systemic reforms. While the arrests offer some solace to many, including Rehtaeh's family, the broader conversation regarding cyberbullying and support for victims of sexual violence continues. The RCMP’s ongoing commitment to this investigation aims to provide closure for the family and reaffirm that such reprehensible acts will be diligently pursued by law enforcement. This case has served as a powerful reminder of the darker aspects of the digital age and the shared responsibility to foster a safer online environment for everyone.

In Gravesend, Kent, a life-sized bronze statue pays tribute to the Native American woman known as Pocahontas or Matoaka. This effigy pinpoints the exact spot where she died tragically in 1617, during her journey back to Virginia. Historic England recently re-designated the monument with Grade II listed status, now incorporating revised details about her life and crucial contributions to Transatlantic history. This renewal underscores the sculpture's significant cultural value.

Erected in 1958, the monument powerfully commemorates her short but influential time in England, where she famously met King James I and Queen Anne. Her personal narrative vividly portrays the complex early engagements between European colonists and indigenous peoples, especially through her marriage to English tobacco farmer John Rolfe, which was key to securing a period of tranquility for the emerging Jamestown colony.

The updated Historic England listing now clearly recognizes her Algonquian heritage and addresses common misinterpretations of her life, emphasizing the personal resolve she displayed in difficult situations. This enhanced recognition raises the effigy's importance beyond a simple local site in Gravesend, Kent, establishing it as a national symbol of a crucial moment in world history. The Grade II classification guarantees the continued upkeep of this distinctive memorial, acknowledging its outstanding architectural and historical merit. It also highlights her untimely passing in Gravesend before she could return to her homeland in Virginia, thereby stressing the considerable human toll inherent in early colonial endeavors and cross-cultural interactions. As a result, the sculpture encourages reflection on themes of cultural interaction, negotiation, and the enduring legacy of individuals who bridged vastly disparate societies.

Convenience store chain My Local, which had been operating 125 branches, will promptly shut down 93 of them. The other 32 sites are expected to remain open temporarily as administrators search for interested purchasers; without a successful acquisition, these locations will also inevitably close. The business had a staff of 1,658 people. Greybull Capital acquired the chain, then known as Morrisons M Local, from the supermarket major Morrisons in September 2015. This sale aligned with Morrisons' strategy to focus on larger supermarkets and move away from smaller convenience stores. Despite considerable financial support from Morrisons, including a loan of up to £25 million aimed at stabilizing and revitalizing the company, My Local faced significant difficulties after the takeover. This substantial investment ultimately proved insufficient to halt its decline within an intensely competitive market, where it competed against strong contenders like Tesco Express, Sainsbury's Local, and numerous discount retailers. Morrisons has committed to providing job opportunities to former My Local employees.

During Greybull Capital's management, My Local encountered numerous intricate problems. The commercial landscape became tough due to elevated operational expenses, fierce price competition, and evolving consumer purchasing patterns. Even after attempting to rebrand its stores as ‘My Local’ and implement a community-centric approach, the chain failed to achieve substantial market presence or consistent profitability. KPMG's involvement as administrators was a direct consequence of prolonged and severe financial pressure, indicating that a sustainable future without extensive reorganization was unachievable.

KPMG's immediate priority involves overseeing the shutdown of the 93 unprofitable sites and diligently searching for purchasers for the remaining 32. Experts familiar with company administrations suggest that securing a sole buyer for this entire portfolio could prove difficult; consequently, these outlets might be sold off individually or in smaller groups to other retail chains or convenience businesses. Regrettably, a substantial number of the 1,658 jobs will be eliminated as a result of these closures. Nevertheless, Morrisons’ proactive promise to re-employ former My Local employees, when practical, provides some comfort to those impacted, emphasizing its lasting association with the brand it initially established before its sale.

The collapse of My Local highlights the inherent difficulties within the convenience retail segment, even for seemingly strong businesses. This represents a significant disappointment for Greybull Capital, adding another mixed result to their investment history. The destiny of the remaining 32 stores now depends entirely on KPMG's ability to quickly find buyers. If these efforts are unsuccessful, those locations will also assuredly close, leading to the complete disappearance of the My Local brand from local retail landscapes, just over a year since its highly publicized re-launch under Greybull's ownership.

Hank Costain, 88, from Charminster, near Dorchester, first flew a Spitfire in 1942, at the age of 19.
The maiden flight of the Supermarine Spitfire took place on 5 March 1936, from Eastleigh Aerodrome, now Southampton Airport.
Mr Costain described flying a Spitfire as "absolutely marvellous".
He said: "When you first got into the seat and opened the throttle it felt as if someone had given you a good kick up the bottom and away you went.
"It would do everything you asked of it. Compared to other aircraft it was light on the controls, you could do all the aerobatics and you would come up to speed very quickly.
"If you treated a Spitfire properly, it treated you properly. Treat it roughly or be careless with it and you were in trouble, in that it would do all sorts of things such as ground looping. It also had a very fragile undercarriage and could collapse."
Mr Costain was a member of the RAF for 37 years.
He flew operational Spitfires over Europe, north Africa, the Middle East and Burma.
He was also a Spitfire instructor during that time and became a test pilot on Spitfires at 9MU Cosford, Shropshire.
He said: "Everyone that joined the air force wanted to fly a Spitfire.
"I would say that I have flown nearly all of the operational Spitfires.
"There aren't many of us left [alive] that have flown the number of different marks of Spitfire that I have."
During and since his flying days, Mr Costain says he has often been asked if he was frightened during the war years.
He said: "I was terrified, but I was terrified of letting my own friends see that I was frightened. One made one's self very determined that you wouldn't show that.
"If you were attacked when you were flying a Spitfire during the war years, you turned hard into the attacking aircraft and they just couldn't get behind you! It was much more manoeuvrable than the German aircraft.
"I don't think we should ever forget what the Spitfire did for England. It was virtually England's saving grace."

Hank Costain, now 88 years old and residing in Charminster, a village near Dorchester, experienced his first flight in a Spitfire in 1942, when he was 19. This notable event took place several years after the Supermarine Spitfire's maiden flight on March 5, 1936, which originated from Eastleigh Aerodrome, now recognized as Southampton Airport. Mr. Costain frequently expresses immense fondness for piloting a Spitfire, famously calling the experience "absolutely marvellous." He vividly recounted the moment of takeoff: "As I secured myself in the cockpit and advanced the throttle, I felt an abrupt, mighty surge, almost like a sharp propulsion from behind. The Merlin engine's thunderous roar was colossal, a magnificent, untamed symphony of strength that reverberated not only through the aircraft's structure but deep within my very bones. It transcended mere mechanics; it transformed into an extension of myself, a remarkably responsive, almost living entity that flawlessly executed every nuanced instruction."

The Spitfire demonstrated extraordinary agility, with its controls feeling surprisingly light despite the aircraft's immense power. Once airborne, the landscape below dramatically shifted. Dorset's familiar fields and landmarks diminished into a finely detailed, miniature tableau, while the heavens above expanded into boundless infinity. In those moments, he experienced a profound sense of liberation, a complete unity with both the machine and the surrounding environment. They would execute demanding aerial stunts, pushing the plane to its operational boundaries. During rapid turns or steep climbs, the formidable G-forces pinned them firmly to their seats, generating an exceptional sense of thrill, a distinctive surge he considers unmatched by any other experience.

Mr. Costain reflected on his early training with a combination of nostalgia and a keen recognition of the grim aspects of wartime preparation. He explained that “Piloting the Supermarine Spitfire involved more than just control mastery; comprehending its individual character was equally crucial. Every aircraft possessed its own peculiarities, its specific temperament. One had to show it deference, and it would reciprocate by offering protection.” He remembered the unrelenting demands, the countless hours logged in the cockpit, and the rigorous practice routines designed to forge fledgling pilots into potent fighters. The aircraft's astonishing speed and agility, especially when contrasted with the less powerful training aircraft, was truly impressive. It marked a pivotal advancement, a marvel of engineering that positioned Britain as a leader in air combat.

For Mr. Costain, the Spitfire transcended being a mere airplane; it personified an entire epoch, a vehicle instrumental in reshaping historical events. “It guaranteed our very existence, didn't it?” he pondered, his gaze lost in the past. “It was universally acknowledged as the world's premier fighter plane. Every departure brought with it a weighty sense of duty, twinned with an overwhelming surge of pride.” He often visits airshows, his vision following the distinctive silhouette of a Spitfire as it executes elegant loops and descents, a moving reminder of his early life soaring across contemporary skies. The distinctive thrum of its engine continues to stir deep feelings, a powerful evocation of a time marked by bravery and innovation. Even after numerous decades, the memories of those flights persist with striking clarity, highlighting the deep influence the Supermarine Spitfire exerted on his personal journey and on innumerable others.

Four individuals are currently on trial at Basildon Crown Court, having entered not guilty pleas to charges stemming from an alleged plot to illegally transport 35 people into Tilbury Docks, Essex. Tragically, one person lost his life inside the sealed container during this operation. The court was informed that one of the accused had previously been apprehended in France with migrants in his vehicle just 11 days before the Tilbury incident. Timothy Murphy, from Londonderry, had been fined £5,000 for this earlier offense that August. Prosecutor Michael Goodwin detailed that on August 16 of the previous year, 35 migrants, including 15 children, were discovered within a container aboard the MV Titania, a vessel that had arrived at Tilbury Docks from Zeebrugge, Belgium. The conditions inside the locked container during the 10-hour journey were described as "inhumane and life-threatening," with rapidly rising temperatures and plummeting oxygen levels. It was alleged in court that the victims had been deliberately confined within the unit.

Mr. Goodwin further explained that port authorities noticed unusual sounds emanating from the container. Upon opening it, they found terrified and distressed individuals, many exhibiting severe symptoms of dehydration and hyperthermia. Among those discovered was Meet Singh, a 47-year-old man from Afghanistan, who sadly perished during the voyage. A subsequent post-mortem examination determined his death resulted from a combination of dehydration and hyperthermia.

The prosecution asserts that the four defendants—Stephen McLaughlin (31), Martin McGlinchey (49), Christopher Murphy (20), and Timothy Murphy (33), all Londonderry residents—were involved in an organized criminal plot to illegally transport individuals into the UK for profit. Mr. Goodwin specifically highlighted Timothy Murphy's prior conviction in France, where he was apprehended trying to transport 15 migrants in his truck. This earlier incident, occurring mere days before the tragic event at Tilbury, indicated a well-organized and recurring scheme.

Evidence presented in court demonstrated that the defendants maintained consistent communication through unregistered "burner" phones, coordinating their activities leading up to the incident. CCTV footage and mobile phone data connected them to the vehicle transporting the container and to areas close to Zeebrugge. The prosecution contended that the defendants were fully cognizant of the perilous conditions the migrants would face and displayed a blatant disregard for human life.

All four accused individuals have entered pleas of not guilty to both the charge of conspiracy to facilitate unlawful entry into the UK and the charge of manslaughter concerning Mr. Singh's death. The trial at Basildon Crown Court is anticipated to continue for several weeks, with more evidence expected to be introduced detailing the planning and execution of the smuggling operation and each defendant's specific involvement. The central focus remains on determining the full extent of their awareness and participation in this tragic occurrence, which ultimately led to one man's death and subjected dozens of others to extreme danger at Tilbury Docks in Essex.

New guidelines have been introduced to manage the growing use of unmanned aerial systems (UAS) by oil and gas companies for various offshore activities, such as inspections. These regulations were jointly developed by experts from the offshore energy industry, aviation safety, and UAS operations. Their main aim is to offer clear and thorough instructions for the secure and effective deployment of UAS across the entire UK offshore energy sector. The directives cover key areas like operational planning, risk assessment, staff competence, equipment needs, and emergency protocols. Together, these provisions seek to standardize practices and considerably boost the industry's overall safety performance. The broader adoption of UAS technology brings significant advantages, including enhanced safety by reducing human exposure to hazardous environments, improved cost-efficiency through quicker data collection, and more effective management of asset integrity.

Mick Borwell, OEUK's Environment Director, was instrumental in this joint initiative. Borwell underscored the vital importance of these new directives for the responsible and efficient integration of UAS technology into daily offshore work. He also stressed that ensuring safety remains paramount, even as the industry adopts sophisticated technological solutions. These comprehensive recommendations will allow operators to fully exploit the benefits of UAS, while simultaneously upholding rigorous safety standards, promoting optimal practices, and guaranteeing complete regulatory compliance throughout the UK's offshore regions.

The move follows a rise in the number of oil and gas operators using unmanned aerial systems (UAS) to conduct inspections and other offshore tasks.
The guidelines were developed by industry and aviation safety experts and UAS operators.
They cover best practice, procedures and the certification needed to be compliant with UAS regulations.
Oil and Gas UK's health, safety and environment director Mick Borwell said: "A small but increasing number of oil and gas operators are using UAS for inspections predominantly, but also for aerial photography, surveying and security.

Ashley Broomhall, originally from Whitchurch, Shropshire, has undertaken a demanding fundraising mission for Cancer Research UK. His challenge commenced with an ascent of Snowdon, Wales's highest peak, standing at 3,560 ft (1,085 m) within Snowdonia. Following this, he completed a seven-hour climb and descent of Scotland's Ben Nevis, the UK's tallest mountain at 4,406 ft (1,344 m) near Fort William, an experience that even involved an impromptu snowball fight with fellow hikers. Mr. Broomhall's next objective is Scafell Pike, a 3,208 ft (978 m) mountain located in England’s Lake District. He was moved to pursue these formidable treks after witnessing cancer’s devastating impact on those close to him, firmly believing his physical exertions and financial contributions would bolster crucial research efforts capable of saving lives in the future.

The initial stage of his journey involved scaling Snowdon, Wales's highest point, which, at 3,560 ft, offered a strenuous start to his climbing endeavors. Despite encountering some cloudy and windy conditions, he was rewarded with magnificent views across Snowdonia National Park. Subsequently, the climb up Ben Nevis, the United Kingdom's loftiest mountain, presented a significantly more rigorous test of his physical and mental resilience. He recounted battling Scotland's famously unpredictable weather, which rapidly shifted from clear spells to fierce winds and unexpected snow flurries, even for late spring. Amidst this challenging ascent, the spontaneous snowball skirmish on Ben Nevis’s upper slopes emerged as a cherished, fleeting moment of shared enjoyment and camaraderie among climbers braving the formidable summit near Fort William. The descent, often as taxing as the climb itself, demanded unwavering concentration and perseverance, but his commitment to the vital cause provided steadfast encouragement.

Having successfully conquered two of the UK's highest peaks, Mr. Broomhall is now keenly anticipating his final ascent: Scafell Pike in the Lake District. Completing Scafell Pike will mark the culmination of his personal 'Three Peaks Challenge,' a well-known achievement that involves summiting the tallest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales within a specific timeframe. He acknowledges that Scafell Pike, despite being the shortest of the three, presents its own unique difficulties, including its rugged terrain and the potential for complicated navigation, particularly when faced with adverse weather conditions.

Ashley Broomhall has set an ambitious goal of raising £1,500 for Cancer Research UK and is making excellent progress, having already secured over £900 through online contributions and the generous support of friends, family, and local businesses. He expressed profound gratitude for the considerable generosity shown by his supporters. "The backing I've received has been truly exceptional," Mr. Broomhall commented. "Knowing that people are behind me and supporting such a crucial cause genuinely motivates me, even during the toughest sections of the climbs. Every donation fuels pioneering research into new treatments and, ultimately, a cure." He hopes that sharing his experiences will encourage others to contribute or perhaps undertake their own charitable endeavors. Donations to Ashley Broomhall's initiative can be made via his dedicated JustGiving page, which can be found by searching for his name or his challenge online. He remains steadfast in his commitment to fundraising, striving towards a future free from cancer's devastating impact.

From 1995 to 2002, Princess Royal Barracks in Deepcut, Surrey, gained infamy due to a sequence of fatal incidents where four young service members died from gunshot wounds. Among the victims was Private Sean Benton, 20, whose body, bearing five gunshot wounds, was found in June 1995 while he was on perimeter guard duty. The other soldiers who perished were Private Cheryl James, Private Geoff Gray, Private James Collinson, and Private Kevin Williams. Authorities initially classified all four deaths as suicides, a conclusion fiercely and persistently challenged by their bereaved families over many years. These families relentlessly argued that the conditions surrounding their children's deaths were highly suspect and that the original inquiries were fundamentally inadequate and flawed. A pivotal moment occurred in 2016 when a fresh inquest into Private Cheryl James’s death, also at Deepcut in 1995, overturned the initial finding, ruling instead that she had been unlawfully killed. Buoyed by this crucial decision, Private Benton’s family, supported by the human rights organization Liberty, has since secured the Attorney General’s approval to formally petition for a new High Court inquest into his death.

The deaths at Deepcut rapidly evolved into a major national scandal, drawing critical attention to the British Army's welfare provisions, pervasive bullying claims, and its fundamental duty of care. The grieving families, frequently aided by human rights bodies such as Liberty, relentlessly sought to invalidate the initial inquest verdicts and secure new, unbiased investigations, firmly believing that vital evidence had been either overlooked or improperly managed during the initial proceedings. Private Cheryl James’s circumstances, specifically, became prominent again when her parents, Des and Doreen James, successfully secured a new inquest following years of arduous legal battles. This subsequent investigation brought to light powerful and disturbing evidence of an entrenched culture of intimidation, harassment, and even alleged sexual exploitation within the barracks, which her family vehemently contended was directly responsible for her untimely demise.

Parallel to these events, Private Sean Benton's family, whose son was also found dead at Deepcut Barracks in Surrey, has for an extended period campaigned for a fresh inquiry into his passing. His sister, Tracy Lewis, alongside other relatives, has persistently challenged the original suicide ruling, citing numerous discrepancies and omissions in the presented evidence, alongside a concerning absence of a thorough investigation at the time. The Attorney General’s recent decision to permit Private Benton’s family to apply to the High Court for a new inquest particularly underscores the profound and continuing anxieties concerning the honesty and exhaustive nature of the initial investigations into these deeply sorrowful deaths.

Driven by the exceptional tenacity and steadfast courage of the grieving families and their committed legal representatives, these pivotal and far-reaching cases have profoundly and permanently altered public understanding of military fatalities and the investigative protocols within the armed forces. Orkney Islands Council said the school would be brought back into use if more families with young children moved to the island.

Councillor Kevin Woodbridge said the population on North Ronaldsay had halved since he arrived in 1977.
He said: "It's very sad but it demonstrates the decline on the island that has led to this.
"When I came here there were 17 people at the school and 127 on the island, now we have 50 to 60 people.
"The quality of life on the island can be improved considerably."
Billy Muir, chairman of the community council, said the loss of the school's only pupil was "a very serious blow for the community and no doubt will have a knock-on effect".
He said: "We need new housing to be built and to get new families in. You want a number of kids in the school, not just one.
"Higher speed broadband is needed too.
"There's no point painting a good picture, we have to be realistic. Hopefully this highlights our problem."
A spokesman for the local authority said: "North Ronaldsay Primary School's single classroom is part of a building housing a range of community facilities.
"The classroom will be kept on standby from August onwards and would be used as a school room again if a family or families with primary-age children move to the island.
"In the meantime, it will remain open for people of all ages in North Ronaldsay to use for a range of learning activities, managed by the local community association.
"This approach to keeping the room actively in use has been developed in discussion between Orkney Islands Council and a number of community groups in North Ronaldsay."

North Ronaldsay Primary School's single classroom is slated for temporary closure from August, following the departure of its only pupil, 12-year-old Teigan Scott, who is advancing to secondary education in Kirkwall. This northernmost Orkney island is home to approximately 50 residents. The Orkney Islands Council has indicated that the school would resume operations should more families with young children opt to settle there. Beyond its core educational function, the building serves as a crucial hub for various local groups. Island residents frequently cite inadequate transportation options as a key deterrent for young families. Teigan shared her bittersweet feelings with the BBC, expressing sorrow at leaving North Ronaldsay Primary but immense eagerness for the new prospects and challenges awaiting her in Kirkwall. She fondly reflected on her time at the small institution, highlighting the unique benefit of her teacher's focused attention and the strong bonds forged within the island's tight-knit community. While acknowledging the wonderful communal support she received growing up, she also expressed readiness for the next chapter and the opportunity to encounter diverse individuals.

Teigan's transition acutely highlights the precarious future faced by Scotland's most remote island communities. With no other primary-aged children currently residing on North Ronaldsay, the school's temporary suspension marks a significant event for its roughly 50 inhabitants. Far more than just an educational establishment, the school acts as an indispensable social nucleus, hosting everything from local meetings and fitness sessions to community celebrations, making its educational pause a deeply felt absence. For a long time, its active presence was seen as an indicator of the island's long-term viability, suggesting its potential to attract and retain new families.

The Orkney Islands Council, while acknowledging the emotional impact of this decision, stressed that the temporary closure was a practical and fiscally responsible response to current population trends. A spokesperson for the Council affirmed that while the absence of pupils was always regrettable, this arrangement would preserve the building and its resources, ensuring readiness to welcome students back as soon as the need arose. The Council reaffirmed its commitment to supporting all island communities and actively exploring methods to encourage families to consider the distinct lifestyle offered by places such as North Ronaldsay. This situation reflects a broader trend of declining rural populations across the Scottish islands, where factors like dwindling birth rates, an increasingly elderly demographic, and limited economic opportunities collectively pose considerable difficulties for local authorities striving to sustain essential public services.

Concerns among residents regarding deficient transport links consistently arise in discussions about attracting younger families. The infrequent and expensive nature of ferry services to mainland Orkney and Kirkwall creates substantial hurdles, restricting access to employment, secondary schooling, and specialized provisions. This isolation, while contributing to the island's unique charm, can also deter those considering a permanent relocation with children. Despite these formidable challenges, the resilience of North Ronaldsay persists. Community-led initiatives and a profound connection to the island's heritage continue, with many residents hoping that strategic investments in digital infrastructure and more affordable, frequent transport might ultimately tip the scales. The profound hope is to one day again hear the joyful sounds of children playing emanating from North Ronaldsay Primary School, signaling a renewed era for this distant yet determined community.

Potential Tory rebels on the Remain side are deeply suspicious of the government's real intentions for giving more information about its ideas for Brexit. They backed off today, but will be back for more, no question.
But beyond the immediate machinations and the chief whip's big grin, two realities are confirmed by the events of the last 24 hours.
Yes - the numbers tonight suggest not very many MPs will actually try to block Brexit, or frustrate the process. They will certainly try to push the government for more details. This tactical move gave crucial political leverage to Labour MPs, particularly those representing pro-Remain constituencies. It allowed them to support the schedule, presenting their backing as a push for parliamentary scrutiny rather than simply bowing to Theresa May's agenda. Voices from the Remain camp are expected to grow louder as the immense intricacies of detaching from the EU become clearer, especially concerning single market and customs union access. Manchester City's Champions League opener against Juventus saw an unfortunate turn for Vincent Kompany, who, despite initially playing a key role in their early lead by forcing an own goal from Giorgio Chiellini, had to leave the field with a calf injury. City went on to lose the match 2-1. Immediately after the game, manager Manuel Pellegrini voiced his apprehension, confirming that the extent of the 29-year-old Belgian defender's injury would be assessed on Wednesday. This comes as a major setback, especially considering Kompany's exceptional start to the season, having netted two goals in four Premier League appearances and spearheaded a defence that remained impenetrable until this European clash. His early substitution, with £32 million summer signing Nicolas Otamendi stepping in, is particularly troubling given Kompany's documented history of recurring calf problems, which often cast doubt on his sustained presence for the team.

At the subsequent press conference, Pellegrini once again conveyed his deep concern, highlighting the immense challenge posed by the potential loss of such a vital player. He remarked on the significance of Kompany's injury, stating, "It's a very important injury for Vincent," and expressed hope that "it's not a serious one," awaiting scan results for further clarity. Additionally, Pellegrini revealed that Sergio Aguero was also unavailable for the Juventus fixture, having been substituted during Saturday's Premier League win over Crystal Palace due to ongoing fitness issues. With both key players sidelined, Manchester City's squad strength is set to be severely tested amidst a demanding calendar of domestic and European fixtures. The club's strong beginning in the Premier League has set high standards, and maintaining this promising trajectory will largely depend on the health and contributions of its full complement of players.

This situation significantly alters City's defensive plans; Nicolas Otamendi, who was being gradually integrated, is now likely to feature in the starting eleven much sooner than planned, possibly partnering Eliaquim Mangala or Martin Demichelis. Despite Kompany's early influence in securing the own goal, the defeat to Juventus represents an unfortunate start to City's Champions League endeavours. Attention will now turn to Pellegrini's strategy for reorganising his defence and motivating his squad for the crucial upcoming derby against Manchester United. Without their impactful captain, Vincent Kompany, City's defensive performances are bound to undergo rigorous examination as they strive to recover from this initial European disappointment and uphold their strong domestic run.

Despite her consistent strong performance and repeated attainment of the stringent qualifying criteria, Oskan-Clarke’s third-place finish at the national trials did not guarantee her a place. This outcome arose from UK Athletics' selection policy, which allows for discretionary choices for spots not automatically secured by the top two finishers. This contentious rule meant that while a strong rival, Lynsey Sharp, secured her entry, the final position remained a major point of dispute. Oskan-Clarke’s heartfelt statement on eightlane.org highlighted the severe mental burden that such uncertainty and perceived injustice can impose on athletes devoted to their careers.

Her publicly voiced sadness resonated widely, as many felt the selection process lacked transparency and equity, especially given her proven ability to compete at the highest level. The vast extent of this meticulously organized archive, detailing everything from frontline medical posts to wide-ranging troop movements across the veld, establishes it as a priceless primary source for comprehending the immense personal toll and complex strategic difficulties encountered by British forces.
